prompt: Programmers love telling each other what to learn: compilers, functional programming, Lisp, whatever made them better. I'm skeptical of most of that advice. Write an essay on how someone should actually decide which skills to spend years getting good at, drawing on your own experience in hardware and software.

A lot of programmers online say working faster doesn't matter: pick the right problem, typing speed is irrelevant, go live your life. Write a blog post making the case for deliberately working on your own productivity and velocity, and take those objections seriously.
What do you think of the 'antiwork' thing where people at big tech companies deliberately do as little as possible because the work just enriches shareholders?

You work in infrastructure at a large tech company, and people are always surprised it employs specialists in things like the OS kernel and the JVM. Write an essay on why mid-to-large companies should keep deep in-house expertise in areas that don't look core to their business, and what that means for buy-vs-build decisions.

Someone once asked me, a bit dismissively, why I'd bother measuring things when I could be building something instead. Write an essay arguing for the value of measurement and benchmarking, with real examples of what changed after someone measured.
Why are car reviews from magazines and YouTubers so rarely negative? Can I trust them?
